steps.tx: **Tuberculous meningitis** is a subacute **basal meningoencephalitis** caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis reaching the subarachnoid space. Symptoms build over 1 to 3 weeks rather than hours, and untreated disease kills rapidly. Treated mortality stays substantial, far higher with HIV coinfection. Tuberculosis behind the blood brain barrier is a medical emergency where treatment must not await confirmation.

steps.tx: Disease begins when a **Rich focus**, a small subpial focus seeded during earlier dissemination, ruptures into the subarachnoid space. Active tuberculosis elsewhere is common, usually pulmonary. Risk concentrates in **HIV infection**, young childhood, old age and contacts of drug resistant strains. Evaluation for tuberculosis elsewhere in the body is mandatory, with HIV testing.

steps.tx: Rupture releases bacilli and antigen into the basal cisterns, where a thick **gelatinous exudate** cakes the pons, optic chiasm, and undersurfaces of the temporal lobes. The exudate strangulates **cranial nerves**, triggers **vasculitis** of the circle of Willis with deep infarction, and blocks cerebrospinal fluid flow to produce **communicating hydrocephalus**. Unlike pure meningitis, bacilli invade the pia and brain itself, so the process is truly a meningoencephalitis.

nodes.label: Nerve, vessel, and CSF flow injury

steps.tx: Low grade fever, malaise and headache creep in first, with Kernig and Brudzinski signs. The bedside giveaway is **cranial nerve involvement**, usually ocular palsies including the **sixth nerve**, with features of raised pressure from hydrocephalus. In infants the neck may stay supple while apathy, irritability, vomiting and seizures dominate. Declining consciousness and seizures demand urgent neurosurgical assessment.

left.title: Adult pattern
points: Fever with headache and behaviour change

steps.tx: Beyond the meninges, tuberculosis builds **tuberculomas**, ring enhancing masses seen with basal enhancement, hydrocephalus and infarcts on imaging. Spinal disease brings cord compression with paraparesis. The closest mimics are partially treated pyogenic meningitis, **cryptococcal** or other fungal meningitis, viral meningoencephalitis and **carcinomatous** meningitis. Contrast imaging plus HIV testing separates them.

steps.tx: Lumbar puncture is the **first test**, showing inflammatory cells with raised protein and low glucose that falls slowly. **Cartridge based nucleic acid amplification** on cerebrospinal fluid gives a rapid answer and detects **rifampicin** resistance, but a negative result never excludes the disease. Contrast imaging shows **basal enhancement** with hydrocephalus, infarcts or tuberculomas, and HIV testing with body evaluation completes the workup.

steps.tx: Treatment is prompt multidrug **anti-tuberculosis therapy** including **rifampicin**, never withheld while awaiting confirmatory tests. Every regimen adds adjunctive **dexamethasone** to reduce mortality and neurological morbidity. Obstructive hydrocephalus needs cerebrospinal fluid diversion with an external drain or shunt. Coinfected patients need HIV care alongside tuberculosis treatment, with monitoring for resistance and raised pressure.

steps.tx: Modern practice starts HIV treatment promptly in coinfected patients and adjusts regimens when **rifampicin** resistance is detected. Obstructive hydrocephalus needs a **ventricular shunt**, expanding tuberculomas need excision for mass effect, and unstable spinal disease needs stabilisation after initial chemotherapy. Seizures and raised pressure need parallel control. Rehabilitation input addresses cognitive impairment, hydrocephalus and paresis.

left.title: Escalated medical care
points: Adjusted regimen when rifampicin resistance is found

steps.tx: Survivors carry risks of **deafness**, blindness, epilepsy, cognitive loss and spinal arachnoiditis with paraparesis. **Dexamethasone** with antibiotics lowers mortality yet disability often persists. Outcome depends heavily on the neurological stage at treatment start: early treatment offers good recovery, while coma and deficits at presentation carry high mortality with frequent lasting sequelae.
